paragraphs: The opening page makes Lin's hesitation visible through objects. On Sunday evening he is smiling at his phone beside books, a mug and the long trailing pothos, joking, "My pothos looks like noodles. Now THAT'S a story." The group chat is asking for a fun Friday lunch story, so he clearly has something he wants to share. Then the test sheet appears with INTROVERT in large type and "Not good at public speaking" highlighted. By the next panel, the metaphor has become physical: Lin is crouched inside a cardboard box marked INTROVERT, saying, "Better not. My type won't allow it." The joke works because the label has shifted from a description on paper into a container he is treating as a rule.

Cilantro provides the comic turning point. At lunch, the cook cheerfully raises a large bunch and announces, "Double cilantro for you!" Lin reacts instantly: "Wait! I have a few things to say!" Three minutes later he is gesturing energetically over the noodles and explaining, "Add that, and the whole bowl belongs to the cilantro!" while the cook answers, "Got it. Not a leaf." Yuan is laughing beside him. The scene does not prove that Lin is secretly some other personality type, and it does not erase his nervousness. It simply gives him a funny piece of evidence that his willingness to speak changes with the subject, the situation and how much he cares about what is being discussed.

The lower page keeps that discovery modest. After lunch, Yuan points back to the contradiction with, "Why didn't your type stop you just now?" Lin replies, "Maybe it hates cilantro too," keeping the joke on the situation rather than turning it into a personality verdict. Walking back to work, he admits, "I'll still get nervous up there." Yuan does not tell him to become outgoing; she suggests a smaller task: "Pick a familiar topic. Just three minutes." That evening, the cardboard box is still in the room, but Lin is now preparing instead of hiding. His line, "Three photos beat a cardboard box," sits beside a notebook listing how he nearly killed the plant, kept it alive, and is still not giving up.

Friday's presentation deliberately shows that progress and discomfort can coexist. Lin stands in front of coworkers with a pothos photo behind him and begins, "Hi, everyone. I..." A small narration box says, "Still nervous. Still here." The next panel is labeled "Three minutes," and the visual payoff returns to the noodle joke: "I tried to grow a forest. I got a bowl of noodles." Someone in the audience asks, "Did it survive?" and Lin answers, "Still trying. Just like me." He has not transformed into a fearless speaker. What has changed is narrower and more believable: he prepared something familiar, stayed through the awkward opening, found a joke that belonged to his real experience, and completed the short share.

The ending does not ask Lin to abandon quietness. Back home, he sits with tea while a cat sleeps by the window, plants fill the room, and he says, "Enough talking for today. A quiet evening tomorrow." The word INTROVERT is now kept in his notebook rather than worn as the front of a box, while the cardboard box has returned to being an ordinary object beside the pothos. The banner says, "Labels are notes, not seals," and the closing line adds, "Names can help. They don't have to write your life." Read alongside the supplied Chapter 32 excerpt, the comic is a contemporary reflection rather than a literal translation: names can help us notice and organize experience, while "knowing when to stop" can also mean noticing the point where a useful name starts becoming a boundary that experience itself does not support.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.title: A Label Can Describe You Without Deciding You
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.teaser: Lin is ready to tell the office about his pothos, which has grown so stringy that it looks like noodles. Then a personality test calls him an INTROVERT and says he is not good at public speaking, so he literally climbs into a cardboard box. The surprise is that cilantro gets him talking, Yuan notices, and a three-minute plant story becomes a small experiment in letting experience add detail to a label.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.quote: As things are first defined, names arise. Once names exist, one must also know where to stop. Knowing where to stop is how one avoids danger.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.practice: Think of one small thing you have postponed because you told yourself, "I'm just not that kind of person." Try a version small enough to give you new information rather than a new identity: choose a familiar topic, give yourself three minutes, or tell one trusted person. Afterwards, write down what actually happened, including both the awkward parts and the easier ones, without rushing to replace the old label with a new one.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.comicTitle: Found Your Type? Don't Box Yourself In
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.comicAlt: A two-page Art Nouveau comic follows Lin, a bespectacled man surrounded by pothos plants, from wanting to share a funny plant story to hiding inside a cardboard box labeled INTROVERT after reading a personality test. A cilantro-heavy lunch unexpectedly gets him talking, Yuan encourages him to try a familiar three-minute topic, and he later gives a nervous but funny office presentation about his noodle-like pothos. The story ends at home with tea, a sleeping cat, the INTROVERT label stored in his notebook, and the message, "Labels are notes, not seals."

listen-before-giving-expertise.title: She Said "I'm Tired." I Built a Management System.
listen-before-giving-expertise.teaser: She says she is tired. He responds with schedules, charts and a mountain of binders. Once he finally listens, even his best advice learns to wait its turn.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible before the advice even arrives. The woman in the loose green blouse is slumped at the desk with one hand against her head, a floral mug and laptop beside her, saying she is tired, cannot get anything done and feels mentally scattered. Across from her, the man in glasses and a white shirt is already typing. She has offered a description of how her day feels; he reacts as though she has handed him a project brief. That mismatch gives the first page its gentle comic tension.

His response then becomes wonderfully excessive. The laptop fills with a color-coded time-management chart, a sleep plan specifying Bed 23:00, Up 7:00 and 8 hours, plus an efficiency section listing Focus, Fewer distractions, Exercise and Daily review. In the next panel, the screen has effectively escaped into the room: huge stacks of binders labeled Time management, Sleep plan and Efficiency system rise across the desk until only the woman's eyes are visible behind them. The more complete the system becomes, the less space she seems to have.

The turning point comes when the woman finally says, "Actually... I just wanted to finish telling you about my day." The man stops and recognizes the mistake himself: he has been answering questions he imagined before listening to what she was actually saying. On the lower page, the change is concrete rather than abstract. He closes the laptop and asks, "Want me to listen first, or help find a solution?" She answers, "Let me finish first." In the next panel he pours tea into her floral mug instead of opening another spreadsheet.

Panel 09 shows what listening looks like in this story. The woman gestures as she explains that two meetings clashed and her lunch went cold; the lunch container is still sitting on the desk as a small, specific proof of the exhausting day she meant to describe. The man listens with his chin resting on his hand. A thought bubble marked "Efficiency plan" appears beside him, but a bold red X crosses it out. The joke is affectionate: the urge to optimize has not vanished, but this time he notices it and lets it pass without interrupting.

The ending shows that the story is not against advice; it changes the timing and permission around it. After the woman says the conversation helped, she later asks how to begin tomorrow's presentation. The man does not unload another system. He first asks, "Want one small tip?" Only after she says yes does he suggest, "Start with a specific example." His final thought—"Even knowledge has to take a number. No cutting in."—turns the lesson into a queueing joke. Read alongside the chapter line about knowing the masculine and keeping to the feminine, the comic can be seen as a contemporary reflection on holding capability without always pushing it forward: strength can include making room, receiving what another person is saying, and waiting until help is actually invited. That is one possible connection, not the only meaning of the ancient text.
listen-before-giving-expertise.quote: Know the masculine, keep to the feminine, and become the valley of the world.
listen-before-giving-expertise.practice: The next time someone says, "I'm tired," you might try one small question before offering a fix: "Do you want me to listen first, or help think through a solution?" If they choose listening, consider closing the laptop, setting the advice aside and letting them finish before deciding what comes next.
listen-before-giving-expertise.comicTitle: She Said "I'm Tired." I Built a Management System.
listen-before-giving-expertise.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Gongbi-style office comic follows a tired woman in green and a man in glasses and a white shirt. After she says she is exhausted, he creates detailed time-management, sleep and efficiency plans until a mountain of binders hides her. She explains that she only wanted to finish talking. He closes the laptop, asks whether she wants listening or solutions, pours tea and hears about clashing meetings and a cold lunch while mentally crossing out an "Efficiency plan." Later she asks for presentation advice; he first asks permission, then gives one small tip: start with a specific example. The closing joke says that even knowledge has to take a number and cannot cut in line.

help-without-taking-over.title: I Came to Help. Then I Took Over Your Life.
help-without-taking-over.teaser: He offered to help with a move. Soon he was choosing the furniture, the curtains and which memories to throw away. An old chair brings him back to his actual job: carrying the boxes.
paragraphs: The opening joke is how quickly a small offer of help expands into a complete takeover. The woman says, "I'm moving next week. A little nervous," and the man in orange workwear immediately answers with routes, van, packing, and everything else. In the next panels he is already pointing across a map marked "Old home" and "New home," presenting a coordinated furniture setup, and holding curtain samples. She is smiling throughout, so the humour comes not from hostility but from his cheerful efficiency gathering momentum faster than anyone asked it to.

The old wooden chair makes the boundary visible. While the surrounding furniture is clean and new, this chair is visibly worn, scratched, and personal. The woman touches it and says that although it is old, it means something to her. The man evaluates it as another logistical problem: too old, space-consuming, uncomfortable, ready to be removed. His reasoning is practical, but that is precisely the comic mismatch—he has become so committed to improving the move that he nearly optimizes away the one object whose value cannot be measured by neatness or convenience.

Panel 06 quietly changes the rhythm. The new room looks orderly, with coordinated curtains, furniture, plants, and moving boxes, yet the woman stands in the middle with her arms open and says, "Lovely... I just feel a bit unnecessary in it." The lower page does not answer this by producing another master plan. Instead, the man sits beside her with his tablet and asks, "So what, exactly, can I help with today?" That question is the turning point: the person receiving help now defines the job instead of being absorbed into somebody else's solution.

From there, the comedy becomes more physical and specific. She points to the heavy box labeled "BOOKS" and says she will choose the rest herself; he rolls up his sleeve and jokes that he is "Back to being the mover." They protect the battered chair together, and his "First class, then" turns the chair from unwanted clutter into an honoured passenger. In the curtain panel, she holds the fabric samples while he keeps the packing tape in his hand and says, "My advice can wait its turn." He is still useful and still funny, but his usefulness no longer requires control.

The final two panels make the change concrete rather than abstract. He carries the book box through the doorway while she positions her old chair where she wants it. Once the work is done, she sits comfortably on that same chair with a cup of tea, while he relaxes on the floor with a water bottle and says, "No life takeover today. Much lighter!" The closing line, "Help carry the boxes. Let them sign for their own life," connects the everyday joke with the supplied Daodejing excerpt as a contemporary reflection: effort can serve another person, but grasping their choices too tightly can defeat the purpose of helping.
help-without-taking-over.quote: Those who act upon it spoil it; those who grasp it lose it.
help-without-taking-over.practice: The next time you feel ready to organize everything for someone, you might first ask, "What, exactly, would you like help with?" Do the part they name, leave the remaining choices with them, and if another excellent suggestion appears, let it wait its turn.
help-without-taking-over.comicTitle: I Came to Help. Then I Took Over Your Life.
help-without-taking-over.comicAlt: Twelve-panel moving-day comic: a man in orange workwear enthusiastically plans a woman's route, furniture, and curtains, then nearly discards her worn old chair. After she says the perfect new home makes her feel unnecessary, he asks what help she actually wants. He carries her books, helps protect the chair, waits while she chooses curtains, and ends seated on the floor with a water bottle while she relaxes in her old chair with tea.

remove-one-extra-goal.title: My Plan Grew Three Kinds of Procrastination
remove-one-extra-goal.teaser: Her goals grow into a tree, but the first day ends without a single word of language practice. Removing one ambitious branch finally gives the others room to grow.
paragraphs: The opening turns an ordinary burst of motivation into a visual joke. The woman in blue announces, "Learn a language! Get fit! Start a channel! Finish my reading list! Starting today!" while her notebook repeats the four-item plan and the black cat watches from beside the desk. In the next panel, the plan has literally grown into a tree: "Language," "Fitness," "Channel," and "Reading list" hang among a clock, camera, books, globe, and other objects. Her delighted "Wow... My plan is growing! So motivating!" captures the funny moment when organizing a future self can already feel like progress.

Panels 03 and 04 show why that excitement becomes heavy. The woman tries to schedule exercise, video work, reading, and language into one packed day while eating at her laptop and handling her phone. Beside her, stacks labeled "Exercise log," "Video script," "Reading list," and "Language notes" rise like physical evidence of productivity. By night she is asleep across the desk next to the black cat, while a clock above the tree appears to melt downward. Her line, "A whole day gone... I still haven't spoken a word. So busy. Still not started," makes the central joke sharper: she has done a great deal around the goals without yet doing the small action she cared about most.

The turning point begins when the man in the red scarf does not offer another elaborate system. He looks at the crowded goal tree and says, "You hung every goal up there. Now you're stuck to the tree. Maybe trim one?" The woman first resists because she worries that choosing less will make her "less well-rounded." In Panel 06 she physically holds the "WELL-ROUNDED" card and asks whether she added it mainly to look impressive. On the lower page, that question becomes a decision: after the man suggests setting aside a goal that is mostly there for appearances, she reaches up and removes the "Channel" tag. The tree remains standing, and the other three goals remain visible.

The space created by that choice immediately becomes concrete rather than heroic. Wearing headphones, the woman speaks to the teacher on her laptop: "Hi! Nice to meet you! I'm nervous, but I finally spoke. Not as scary as I thought!" The teacher on screen answers, "Nice to meet you!" and her notebook records the modest achievement "Today: Spoke once." In the next panel she stretches beside the black cat while her checklist shows language practice and thirty minutes of exercise checked off, with the reading list still honestly marked "in progress." Nothing in the image suggests that she has mastered everything; the comedy and relief come from two real actions finally replacing a mountain of preparation.

The ending keeps the trade-off gentle rather than absolute. The man says that one less goal leaves more room for what she actually wants, and the woman replies, "Setting it aside wasn't failure. It made space for what matters." In the final panel she sits peacefully with a mug and the black cat beneath the tree, looking toward a bright city skyline. Only "Language," "Fitness," and "Reading list" remain hanging beside the softly distorted clock, and she says, "One less wish hanging on it. Now the tree can grow." The closing line, "Some wishes can wait. Let the ones that matter begin," connects naturally with Chapter 42's paradox of loss and gain without claiming that everyone should always pursue fewer goals; here, this particular character benefits from distinguishing what matters now from what can wait.
remove-one-extra-goal.quote: Some things are increased by being diminished; increased, they may instead be diminished.
remove-one-extra-goal.practice: Look at today's task list and notice whether one item is there mainly to make the plan look more complete rather than because it needs your attention now. Consider setting that one aside for ten minutes, then use the space for one small beginning you genuinely want: say one sentence in another language, take a short walk, or read one page with full attention.
remove-one-extra-goal.comicTitle: My Plan Grew Three Kinds of Procrastination
remove-one-extra-goal.comicAlt: A twelve-panel surreal comic follows a woman in blue whose four ambitions grow into a literal goal tree. After a packed day leaves her exhausted and still not speaking her target language, a man in a red scarf helps her question the "WELL-ROUNDED" goal. She removes the "Channel" tag, speaks "Hi! Nice to meet you!" to a teacher on her laptop, checks off language practice and thirty minutes of exercise, and ends beneath the tree with her black cat, a mug, three remaining goal cards, melting clocks, and a peaceful city skyline.

reading-a-difficult-line.title: Read Three Pages, Bought Eight Books
reading-a-difficult-line.teaser: Three pages in, he buys eight more books. Then come the highlighters. One honest question and a sour mango finally move him beyond looking like a reader.
paragraphs: The opening makes the scale of his ambition part of the joke. Sitting at the table with The Meaning of Life, the man announces, "Tonight, I'm going to figure out life." Only three minutes later, his posture has collapsed into his hand and a question mark hangs above him: "I know every word. Still don't understand life." The room, book, mug, lamp and nighttime skyline barely change; what changes is the distance between recognizing words and understanding what they are trying to say.

Instead of staying with that difficulty, he builds an impressive support system around it. The next panel fills the table with Intro to Philosophy, Western Philosophy, Key Concepts Dictionary, Multiple Perspectives, Classics Guide, Cultural Context and Evolution, Modern Thinkers and Interviews with Thinkers. His punch line is that if one book is unclear, he clearly has not "BOUGHT" enough books. Then the colored highlighters appear, covering the open pages so thoroughly that the woman asks whether he is reading the book or decorating it. The humor comes from how productive all this preparation looks while the original confusion remains untouched.

The book-club scene changes the direction without pretending the problem has vanished. In front of the CITY BOOK CLUB sign, the man arrives carrying his stack and holds up a sheet marked "PROFOUND," declaring, "This is... profound." The woman simply asks, "Which line, exactly?" In the next panel the performance drops: the paper now carries a large question mark, and he admits, "This line. I don't understand it." Her answer, "Good. Now we have somewhere to start," turns vagueness into one concrete place they can actually examine together.

The mango sequence gives that distinction a physical joke. The package announces "SWEET," while a real mango and bright slices sit on the plate. The woman asks whether he has actually tasted it; in the following panel his tightly squeezed eyes and puckered, sour face answer more convincingly than the label ever could. Her line, "Sweet label. Honest face," keeps the point playful: a word can indicate something, but the word is not the whole encounter. The comic then returns to the open book, where a hand writes "What does this line mean?" on a sticky note while the woman suggests leaving one question for today.

The ending deliberately avoids instant enlightenment. In the kitchen, the man cuts mango for dinner and says, "Dinner doesn't have to wait for all the answers." A week later he is back at the same book, with the mango bowl nearby and a question-mark bookmark still sticking out of The Meaning of Life. He says only, "I think I understand a little more this time." The closing line, "Leave a question open. Give yourself a reason to turn the page," fits the visible change: not total mastery, but a willingness to return. As a contemporary reflection on Chapter 1, the story echoes the tension between what can be named or said and what remains larger than the name, without treating the comic as a literal translation of the ancient text.
reading-a-difficult-line.quote: A Dao that can be spoken of is not the constant Dao.
reading-a-difficult-line.practice: Choose one line you genuinely do not understand and write down one specific question about it. First say, in your own words, what you think you read; then test that reading against one ordinary example. You do not have to settle the question today. Leave it visible and return to it later.
reading-a-difficult-line.comicTitle: Read Three Pages, Bought Eight Books
reading-a-difficult-line.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Ligne Claire comic shows a man trying to understand The Meaning of Life: he buys a stack of explanatory books, covers pages in highlighter, admits at a city book club that he does not understand one line, tests the gap between the word "SWEET" and a sour-tasting mango, leaves a question on a sticky note, cooks dinner, and returns to the book the next week with a question-mark bookmark, saying he understands a little more.

different-strengths.title: Our Sports Day Almost Became a Beauty Contest
different-strengths.teaser: Rank everyone by running speed. Even basketball. What could go wrong? Three coworkers discover that the best runner and the best team are very different things.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visual before it is philosophical. The tall yellow-shirt man with glasses announces an "all-round champion" while holding a ruler beside the red-shirt man, then proposes ranking everyone by running time. The red-shirt man immediately spots the mismatch: "Even basketball gets scored by running?" He really is fast in the next panel, charging across the track ahead of the blue-hoodie woman, but that strength belongs to a particular task rather than automatically becoming a universal measuring stick.

The basketball panel makes that mismatch concrete. The red-shirt man sends the ball sailing toward what looks like a target, only for the blue-hoodie woman to point out, "Nice shot. Shame that basket has a lid." The object is visibly a lidded trash bin, so the humour comes from applying confidence and athletic energy in the wrong setting, not from denying that he can run. The following relay scene pushes the same problem further: runners rush ahead while the yellow-shirt man is left holding a bundle of batons and asking why nobody waited for him.

The first page ends not with a victory but with three disappointed coworkers sitting behind a row of mismatched trophies. The red-shirt man sums up the problem: "We picked the fastest people. We didn't pick a team." That line turns the story away from individual rankings. The trophies are still there, but their variety now looks slightly absurd beside a group whose actual difficulty is coordination. Nothing in the scene claims that speed is bad; it simply shows that several impressive individual results have not yet solved the shared task.

The turning point comes when the blue-hoodie woman changes the question. In front of a diagram labeled "Sprint," "Stay steady," and "Pass it on," she asks, "First, what does this stage need?" The relay that follows gives those labels physical meaning. She receives a baton steadily, the yellow-shirt man directs from the side with a megaphone, and in the next panel she deliberately says, "I slow down here so you can speed up next." Slow and fast stop behaving like rival labels and become connected parts of one exchange.

By the finish-line panel, all three are crossing together, and the yellow-shirt man observes that someone has to pick up where another person leaves off. Back at work, the joke returns to the original measuring obsession: the red-shirt man works quickly at his laptop, the blue-hoodie woman examines pages with a magnifying glass, and the line "Finally. No more judging copy with a ruler." turns the old standard into an office gag. The final framed certificate reads "ALL-ROUND TEAM," while the yellow-shirt man still holds the ruler and says, "Different strengths. One whole team." Read alongside Chapter 2, this is not a literal translation of the text but a contemporary illustration of relational qualities: what counts as long, short, fast, slow, strong, or useful becomes clearer through contrast, context, and connection.
different-strengths.quote: Long and short give shape to each other.
different-strengths.practice: Think of one shared task you are working on and name the different stages it actually requires. Before deciding who is "best," ask what each stage needs, then notice whether one person's slower, steadier, or more careful move makes the next person's work easier.
different-strengths.comicTitle: Our Sports Day Almost Became a Beauty Contest
different-strengths.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Bauhaus-style office sports-day comic follows a red-shirt runner, a blue-hoodie woman, and a tall yellow-shirt man with glasses. A single running-speed standard fails across basketball and relay events; the team then maps different roles, coordinates a baton exchange, crosses the line together, and returns to office work where a magnifying glass, ruler joke, and "ALL-ROUND TEAM" certificate replace the earlier obsession with one universal measure.

shopping-after-scrolling.title: My Life Is Just One Juicer Away
shopping-after-scrolling.teaser: A late-night scroll promises a better life, delivered with a juicer. Two minutes of drinking and thirty minutes of washing later, a friend offers an orange—and a pause before the next purchase.
paragraphs: The joke begins in panel 01 with an extremely ordinary promise: the brown-haired woman lies under a pink blanket beside the sleeping calico cat and tells herself, "One quick look. Then sleep." Her phone is already showing glossy green-drink imagery, and the next panel immediately enlarges that tiny scroll into a fantasy morning of bright windows, a city skyline, a yoga mat, sunshine, and a green juice in hand. The contrast is the first visual punch line: she is still in bed, but the advertisement has already furnished an entire future for her.

Panels 03 through 06 make that fantasy increasingly physical. Sitting in a cluttered room with a notebook, she decides, "No wonder I lack discipline. I don't own a juicer." At 00:23 she taps "ORDER NOW" while declaring, "Buy a machine. Get a whole new life delivered." Three days later, her striped-shirt friend arrives to find boxes labeled "JUICER," "YOGA MAT," and "JOURNAL," turning self-improvement into a literal warehouse joke. Then the bright promise meets the kitchen counter: the woman, now in pink pajamas, sits beside a juicer, dirty parts, fruit scraps, peels, bowls, and dishes, sighing that two minutes of drinking have produced thirty minutes of washing.

The second page does not declare the juicer a mistake. Instead, panel 07 shows the next recommendation arriving before the first purchase has even settled into daily life: an "AUTOMATIC JUICER CLEANER." The brown-haired woman wonders, "Maybe I still need one more thing..." while her friend looks on. The turning point comes in panel 08, where the striped-shirt friend simply holds out an orange and asks, "Do you want juice, or do you want that morning?" The nearby "GOOD THINGS TAKE TIME" poster quietly reinforces the pause without turning the conversation into a lecture.

Panels 09 through 11 shift attention from upgrading the setup to testing the desire. In warm daylight, with the calico cat nearby, the woman peels and eats an actual orange and jokes, "Turns out sunshine has no minimum order." She then writes "CHECK TOMORROW" in a notebook, listing the automatic cleaner and a sports bottle, while her friend suggests letting the impulse "work a night shift" in the cart. The next day, the cleaner is crossed out but the sports bottle remains checked. That detail matters: the comic does not treat every purchase as foolish. One accessory loses its urgency overnight, while something she still finds useful stays on the list.

The ending returns to the morning she originally wanted, but without pretending that life has been perfected. In panel 12 the two women sit together laughing over oranges, a plate of orange wedges, mugs, and the still-visible juicer at the side of the table. The brown-haired woman says, "Today I'll just live. No upgrade required." The closing line, "Spend less time on what you're missing. Notice the life you already have," connects the story loosely to Chapter 3's concern with desire and external stimulation: not as a literal translation of the ancient text, and not as a rule against buying things, but as an invitation to notice how easily a displayed object can arrive bundled with an imagined identity or lifestyle.
shopping-after-scrolling.quote: Do not put desirable things on display, so that the people are not thrown into disorder.
shopping-after-scrolling.practice: Put one thing you suddenly want into a "check tomorrow" list. The next day, write down the specific problem it would solve and the effort of using, cleaning, storing, or maintaining it. If a simple option is already available, try that once first; if the purchase still makes sense afterward, keep it.
shopping-after-scrolling.comicTitle: My Life Is Just One Juicer Away
shopping-after-scrolling.comicAlt: Two-page Pop Art comic with halftones and bold red, yellow, and cyan accents. A brown-haired woman scrolls in bed beside a calico cat, imagines a sunny disciplined life with green juice, orders a juicer at 00:23, and later faces boxes, fruit scraps, and dirty juicer parts. Her striped-shirt friend offers an orange and asks whether she wants juice or the imagined morning. The woman delays an automatic juicer cleaner overnight, crosses it off the next day while keeping a sports bottle, and ends by sharing oranges with her friend in a bright kitchen.

one-knot-at-a-time.title: My Earbud Cable Has Better Social Skills Than I Do
one-knot-at-a-time.teaser: His earbud cable has befriended his keys, access card and a hair tie. Pulling harder only tightens the party. One small knot—and no new group chats—might be a better start.
paragraphs: The opening joke is completely physical: the man in the green hoodie pulls a ridiculous knot of white earbuds, a USB cable, keys, an access card, and other small objects from his backpack and announces, "My earbuds made new friends. Again." The woman in cream overalls leans toward the mess and replies that their social circle is bigger than his. Because the objects really are wrapped around one another, the social metaphor grows directly out of the picture rather than being pasted onto it.

His first response is to treat the tangle as one giant emergency. In panel 03 he pulls hard in both directions and declares, "I'm fixing all of this. Right now!" By panel 04, the same knot sits on the table while his phone adds BILL, MEETING, and PARCEL notifications, so one cable has become a visual stand-in for several demands arriving together. The scissors in panel 05 push that impulse toward comic excess, while the woman's glass of water and dry line, "Bit harsh on the earbuds," bring the scale of the response back down.

The real turn happens without a dramatic breakthrough. In panel 06 the man simply asks where to start, and the woman points to one specific place in the knot: "Right here." Panel 07 moves in close on his hands loosening a single small knot, with the line "Loosen first. Win later." The next panel makes progress visible rather than magical: the keys and blue ACCESS card are now free, and the woman jokes, "First friend: checked out." Nothing has been solved all at once, but the pile is already less entangled.

The comic then carries the same method into ordinary responsibilities. In panel 09, BILL, MEETING, and PARCEL appear as separate paper slips while the man says, "One problem first. No all-hands meeting for my entire life." Panel 10 makes the idea spatial again: the earbuds are neatly coiled with a cable tie, the backpack has an open compartment, and the woman says, "Give them space. No new group chats." The humor works because organization is shown as literal separation, not as a sudden transformation of his entire life.

The ending keeps that modest scale. In panel 11 the man heads out with his backpack, keys in hand and earbuds usable again, saying, "Not everything's fixed. But I can finally move." Panel 12 leaves the USB cable beside the pink hair tie while the woman points between them and warns, "You two. No adding friends yet." The closing line, "Loosen one knot. Give the rest some room to move," offers a contemporary reflection on the chapter's language about blunting sharpness and untangling confusion: not a literal translation of the ancient text, but a playful image of reducing force, distinguishing what is actually connected, and creating room for movement.
one-knot-at-a-time.quote: Blunt its sharpness; untangle its knots; soften its light; mingle with the dust.
one-knot-at-a-time.practice: You might write down the things that currently feel tangled together, then choose one small part that can move without waiting for everything else. Try that piece first. If pushing harder only tightens the situation, see whether one assumption, dependency, or connection can simply be loosened.
one-knot-at-a-time.comicTitle: My Earbud Cable Has Better Social Skills Than I Do
one-knot-at-a-time.comicAlt: A twelve-panel torn-paper collage comic follows a man in a green hoodie and a woman in cream overalls dealing with a tangled bundle of earbuds, a USB cable, keys, an access card, and a pink hair tie. He first pulls at the knot, gets overwhelmed by BILL, MEETING, and PARCEL notifications, and considers scissors. She redirects him to one small knot. The keys and access card are freed, the daily tasks are separated onto paper slips, the earbuds are coiled with a cable tie, space is left in the backpack, and he heads out saying he can finally move. In the final panel, she points between the loose USB cable and hair tie and jokes that they should not add each other as friends yet.

leave-room-in-conversation.title: I Turned a Friendly Chat into a Customer Hotline
leave-room-in-conversation.teaser: A friend comes for tea. Within minutes, she has a headset and three solutions; he still has not finished a sentence. Then customer support goes off duty, and the real conversation begins.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built from escalation. The woman begins warmly with "How have you been?" while pouring tea, but the next panel stacks three bubbles above the man: "Work?", "Love life?", and "Sleeping okay?" His tiny "..." makes the imbalance visible. By panel 3 she is already promising, "Don't worry! I'll work it out for you!" before he has explained anything. The care itself is not mocked; the comedy comes from how quickly a casual visit starts behaving like an intake form.

Panel 4 makes that metaphor literal. The woman appears with a headset and holds up a flowchart offering three numbered routes while announcing, "For your problem, I have three solutions." The man is still simply holding his mug. In panel 5 he tries to begin with "Actually...", only to be overtaken by the enormous "I GET IT!" beside him. The visual gag is precise: the more confidently the conversation gets solved, the less room he has to finish a sentence.

The turning point arrives when the man raises his hand and says, "Don't get it yet. Let me finish loading." The computer-language joke keeps the correction light, but the boundary is clear. On the second page, the woman's response is not another improved technique or a fourth solution. She lowers the chart and says, "Okay. Take your time." Then panel 8 contains no dialogue at all: both characters simply sit on the sofa and drink steaming tea. The comic lets the pause itself become part of the action.

Only after that quiet panel does the man explain, "I'm not looking for a fix. I'm just tired." The woman answers, "Then we don't have to solve it today." A small prop change carries the idea further: the once-important flowchart is now lying flat on the coffee table underneath her cup. In panel 11, he says that saying it aloud helps a little, while she answers only, "I'm listening." The story does not turn her into a distant observer; it shows her staying engaged without turning every sentence into a task.

The supplied line from Chapter 5 offers a useful image for reading this ending without making the comic a literal translation of the text. Something can remain open without being useless, and movement can allow more to emerge. Here, conversational space works in that spirit: once every silence is no longer filled with questions, diagnosis, or advice, the man's actual words have somewhere to appear. The final panel makes the joke concrete again: the headset hangs on an empty chair beside the sunset window while the two friends sit together facing the view. "Customer support is off duty. Your friend is still here." The closing line, "Leave one sentence unsaid. You might hear a whole person.", turns the abandoned hotline into a quieter form of companionship.
leave-room-in-conversation.quote: Empty, yet it is not exhausted; set in motion, it brings forth ever more.
leave-room-in-conversation.practice: The next time someone brings up a difficulty, you might first ask, "Would you like me to listen, or would you like us to think through options together?" If they pause, try leaving that pause open for a moment before adding your own experience. The point is not to say less at all costs, but to give their next sentence room to arrive.
leave-room-in-conversation.comicTitle: I Turned a Friendly Chat into a Customer Hotline
leave-room-in-conversation.comicAlt: Two-page minimalist twelve-panel comic in warm neutral tones. A bob-haired woman in a white blouse and black trousers meets a man in a black sweater and cream trousers for tea on a sofa. She rapidly asks about work, love life, and sleep, then puts on a customer-service headset and presents a three-option flowchart. When he tries to say "Actually...", she interrupts with "I GET IT!" He raises a hand and asks her to let him finish loading. On the second page she lowers the chart, they share a silent cup of tea, and he finally says he is not looking for a fix and is simply tired. She replies that they do not have to solve it today. The chart ends up under a cup on the table, she tells him "I'm listening", and the final panel shows them from behind watching a sunset city view while the headset rests on an empty chair.

keep-a-small-ritual.title: My Self-Discipline Fits in a Flowerpot
keep-a-small-ritual.teaser: Tomorrow: running, reading, piano, a whole new person. By day three, even the plant is struggling. A neighbour brings a watering can—and a much smaller place to begin.
paragraphs: The opening joke is built into the contrast between the young woman's confidence and the room's immediate reply. In panel 01, she pins up a beautifully decorated "MY NEW PLAN" with RUN, READ, and PIANO waiting in neat rows while declaring, "Starting tomorrow, I'll be a whole new person." Panel 02 answers with a phone at her ear, a laptop or folder wedged against her body, shopping bags, parcels, loose papers, and the black-and-white cat watching the pile-up from below. Her line, "The new me isn't here yet. The old workload is," turns the ambitious makeover into a visual collision between an ideal schedule and an already crowded life.

By "Day Three," the comedy has gone quiet. The young woman sits curled on the floor in patterned socks, surrounded by crumpled paper, an open notebook, and a mug, while the same plan still hangs behind her and the red heart pot by the window is visibly wilted. "Failed again" makes several unchecked ambitions feel like one sweeping verdict. The turning point arrives when the gray-haired neighbour appears in her blue floral apron holding the blue watering can. She asks only, "Watered your plant today?" The young woman answers, "I can't even manage my life," but the neighbour does not add another life-management system to the wall.

Panel 05 lowers the scale of the problem with a wonderfully literal prop: the neighbour simply passes over the watering can and says, "The plant didn't ask you to sort out your whole life first." In panel 06, the young woman waters the still-drooping plant and asks, "That's it?" while the neighbour, chin resting comfortably on her hand, replies, "That's it for today." The black-and-white cat remains nearby as a quiet witness. Nothing has suddenly transformed: the leaves are not magically lush, the checklist is not completed, and there is no triumphant montage. The joke is that the supposedly enormous project of becoming disciplined has, for the moment, become one very ordinary minute with a flowerpot.

The second page keeps that smallness without turning it into another rigid rule. Before leaving with her backpack, the young woman checks the plant and says, "Not thirsty today? I'll just say hello," so care means observing its condition rather than automatically watering it. Later, beside a laptop, stacks of work, a desk lamp, and the attentive cat, she wipes a leaf and notices that "A small thing can actually wait for me." The calendar in "Sometimes I Forget" makes the next joke explicit: red marks fill several days, one square is left open, and her response is "Missed yesterday. No detention today." Continuity here includes gaps instead of treating every missed day as a disciplinary hearing.

The ending shows change through details rather than a victory speech. The young woman peers through a magnifying glass at a fresh leaf while the neighbour says, "Growth isn't a daily performance." In "A Smaller Plan," the familiar RUN, READ, and PIANO list remains, but "Two pages today still counts" replaces the earlier demand for a total reinvention. Finally, at sunset, she reads beside the healthier plant while the black-and-white cat sleeps on the floral cushion, saying, "My self-discipline isn't impressive. But it's alive." As a contemporary association with Chapter 6, this fits the image of something continuing quietly without being forced into spectacle: the comic does not claim to translate the ancient line literally, but it imagines continuity as an action small enough to remain available tomorrow.
keep-a-small-ritual.quote: It goes on, as though barely present; use it, and it is never exhausted.
keep-a-small-ritual.practice: Choose one small action that can fit inside the day you already have, perhaps two pages, one checked leaf, or one minute of tidying. Let it become smaller when the day is crowded, and if you miss it once, simply notice where you are and continue when it makes sense. After a few days, check whether the action still fits rather than turning it into another test.
keep-a-small-ritual.comicTitle: My Self-Discipline Fits in a Flowerpot — Chapter 6
keep-a-small-ritual.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel Nordic folk-art comic with grainy paper texture, floral bird decorations, and a cozy apartment setting. A braided young woman in a red cardigan begins with a large RUN, READ, and PIANO checklist, then arrives overwhelmed by work, bags, packages, and a phone call. By day three she sits among crumpled papers beside a wilting plant in a red heart pot. A gray-haired neighbour in a blue floral apron offers a watering can and suggests caring for the plant without first fixing her whole life. The young woman waters it briefly, later checks whether it is thirsty, wipes a leaf during a busy evening, misses a calendar day without punishment, inspects a new leaf with a magnifying glass, scales her reading goal down to two pages, and ends reading peacefully at sunset beside the plant and a sleeping black-and-white cat.

credit-the-quiet-work.title: I Got the Trophy. The Whole Team Lost Sleep.
credit-the-quiet-work.teaser: He holds the trophy beneath a giant ME. His teammates hold cables, plans and the work that made it happen. A better photograph begins with a more honest account of the project.
paragraphs: The opening makes its joke visually before anyone corrects the project lead. He stands under bright stage lights with the trophy, while the enormous word "ME" dominates the presentation screen behind him. His line, "I put a lot into this project," is not false, but the composition makes his first-person framing comically oversized. The next panel cuts backstage, where Qing stands beside equipment and Chen is literally holding a thick coil of cable, with takeout containers and production clutter nearby. Qing's remark that he put a lot of "me" into it turns the contrast between polished stage and unseen labour into the first punch line.

The office scenes make that hidden work concrete rather than abstract. The lead sits amid stacks of papers and books, with the trophy still visible nearby, while sticky notes name RESEARCH, DISCUSSION, DESIGN, REVISIONS, and TESTING. Qing and Chen then open plans and diagrams across the desk, and Chen jokes, "What did you think was in the trophy? Air?" The humour works because the award is physically present beside all the evidence of work that made it possible. In the following phone photograph, the lead notices how centrally he has placed himself while teammates are squeezed around him, turning his earlier way of telling the story into a visible problem of composition.

The lower page changes the behaviour rather than merely changing the speech. On the presentation slide, Qing is identified with DESIGN, Chen with DELIVERY, and the lead with COORDINATION. He then steps aside and says, "Let's hear this part from the people who did it." Qing and Chen take the microphones and explain their work while he sits at the side taking notes. Importantly, the comic does not erase his contribution: when questioned later, he says, "My job was making these pieces connect." The correction is therefore not that he did nothing, but that coordination is one real contribution among several real contributions.

The ending makes the new balance visible through objects and body placement. In the new team photograph, Qing, the lead, and Chen stand shoulder to shoulder, with the trophy shared at the centre of the table instead of functioning as a solitary badge. The lead jokes, "This time, no imaginary coworkers needed," a playful reversal of the earlier framing in which the team's labour had almost disappeared from his story. In the final panel, they are back around plans, laptops, pens, sticky notes, and coffee mugs. Chen proposes talking together from the start of the next project, while the lead answers, "Shared the credit. Got a stronger team."

The supplied passage from Chapter 7 speaks of Heaven and Earth enduring because they do not exist only for themselves. The comic uses that idea as a contemporary reflection on collaboration, not as a literal translation of the ancient text. Its closing line, "Step back a little. Let everyone's work be seen," is enacted visually: the lead remains present, names his coordinating role, and still helps connect the work, but no longer occupies the whole frame. The story does not promise that giving credit automatically produces loyalty or success; it simply shows how more accurate recognition can make a shared project feel genuinely shared.
credit-the-quiet-work.quote: The reason Heaven and Earth can endure and last is that they do not live for themselves; therefore they can endure for a long time.
credit-the-quiet-work.practice: Think of one recent result you presented or celebrated. Write down one specific piece that someone else researched, designed, delivered, revised, tested, organized, or supported. In your next update or thank-you, name that contribution clearly while also stating, just as clearly, the part you were responsible for.
credit-the-quiet-work.comicTitle: I Got the Trophy. The Whole Team Lost Sleep.
credit-the-quiet-work.comicAlt: A two-page, twelve-panel risograph comic in blue, orange, yellow, and cream. A curly-haired man in an orange shirt accepts a trophy onstage beneath a giant "ME," while backstage Qing, a bob-haired woman in blue, and Chen, a glasses-wearing man in yellow, handle cables, production work, plans, and leftover takeout. At the office, stacks of documents and sticky notes marked RESEARCH, DISCUSSION, DESIGN, REVISIONS, and TESTING reveal the team's work. After noticing how his own framing has crowded the others, the lead returns to the stage with a slide assigning DESIGN to Qing, DELIVERY to Chen, and COORDINATION to himself. Qing and Chen present while he takes notes, and he later explains that his role was connecting the pieces. The final panels show the three together around the shared trophy and then planning the next project around a table with drawings, laptops, coffee, pens, and sticky notes. The page closes with "Step back a little. Let everyone's work be seen."

explaining.title: This Misunderstanding Is Not Getting a Sequel
explaining.teaser: One sent receipt becomes three seasons of explanation. He wants the file understood—and his innocence officially applauded. A tied-up paper scroll marks where the sequel stops.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible before the man even starts defending himself. The woman asks, "Why didn't you send it?" while the laptop directly in front of them already displays "SENT." Instead of letting that small piece of evidence do its job, he begins, "Let me start with Monday..." A single misunderstanding immediately grows into a long paper scroll that curls across the desk. By Panel 03, the scrolls have multiplied so dramatically that the woman's question, "Is this a reply or a serial novel?" becomes both the verbal joke and the visual one.

The middle of the first page shows what has quietly changed. The man is no longer only trying to establish what happened; he is staring at his phone and asking, "Why hasn't he admitted I was right?" The papers keep growing because the desired result has also grown. In Panel 05, the woman holds up the short "SENT" receipt while asking, "Are you adding facts, or waiting for a verdict?" Then Panel 06 makes the contrast deliberately absurd: the man holds one small screenshot in one hand and an armful of rolled explanations in the other, smiling as he admits, "One screenshot. I wrote three seasons."

The second page changes the scale of his response rather than pretending the misunderstanding never existed. In Panel 07, both his speech bubble and the enlarged phone message say, "I sent the file yesterday. Forwarding it again now." The giant paper saga has been replaced by one clear factual sentence and a concrete next step. When a "NEW REQUEST" appears in Panel 08, he does not absorb it silently or treat it as part of the old dispute. He states, "I'll schedule the additions tomorrow," making the boundary visible while continuing the work.

Panels 09 through 11 show that stopping the argument is not the same as withdrawing. The man places his phone down, and the woman, surprised by the lack of another explanatory installment, asks, "No follow-up question?" He answers while writing, "I can explain it clearly. I can't nod for him." The wording keeps responsibility divided: he can make his own communication clear, but he cannot manufacture another person's agreement. The next panel confirms that ordinary life continues—the laptop is open, the work is moving, and the phone gives only the modest acknowledgement "RECEIVED." The woman jokingly asks, "The grand finale?" but the receipt is not presented as an apology, victory, or complete agreement.

The final panel closes the recurring joke with a physical change on the desk. Instead of being buried under loose scrolls, the man calmly drinks tea beside a single long paper roll that has been tied shut. When he says, "No. This is simply where I stop," the comic does not suggest silence, surrender, or refusing to resolve misunderstandings. He has already stated the facts, resent the file, set a schedule for new work, and returned to what he can actually do. Read alongside Chapter 8, the ending offers a contemporary reflection on non-contention: not eliminating clear expression, but reducing the extra struggle to force a particular acknowledgement after one's own part has been done.
explaining.quote: Precisely because he does not contend, he is free from blame.
explaining.practice: When you feel an explanation turning into another episode, separate the facts you still need to communicate from the response you hope to receive. State the facts and the next step briefly, keep any necessary boundary clear, and then consider returning your attention to the part that remains yours to do.
explaining.comicTitle: This Misunderstanding Is Not Getting a Sequel
explaining.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Chinese ink-wash-style office comic on warm paper. A messy-haired man in a gray shirt responds to a short-haired woman in an ochre shirt after a file is questioned despite a visible "SENT" receipt. His explanations expand into absurd curling paper scrolls until she compares them to a serial novel and asks whether he wants to add facts or wait for a verdict. On the second page he sends one concise message, schedules a new request for tomorrow, puts down his phone, continues working after a simple "RECEIVED," and finally drinks tea beside the enormous explanation roll tied shut, saying, "No. This is simply where I stop."
